title: Solving Linear and Integer Programs Faster Using Data
claim: When the cost region restricts which optimizers are reachable, the problem reduces to a lower-dimensional subspace without losing any optimal solution.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right, cost space mapped to decision space
description: Two side-by-side 2-D coordinate plots on a white background. The left panel, labeled 'Cost space', has gray axes c1 and c2. A dashed blue shaded rectangle, labeled C_rho, sits left of the c2 axis. It spans c1 from -1-rho to -1, and a double-headed arrow marks its width rho. The right panel, labeled 'Decision space', shows a light-gray square X spanning [-1,1]^2 with black edges. Its right edge is a thick red line labeled X*(C_rho) and x=(1,z). A red upward arrow labeled U sits inside the square, parallel to that edge. A dot marks the origin. The eye goes first to the red edge and arrow, which contrast with the muted gray axes and the pale blue region. No arrow links the panels, so the reader infers the mapping from the shared colors and notation.
caption: Exact compression through the decision-relevant subspace. Costs in $\C_\rho$ have $c_1<0$, so all reachable optimizers lie on the highlighted right edge. The direction $U=(0,1)^\top$ parameterizes this edge as $x=(1,z)$, reducing the LP to one variable while preserving its full optimizer set.
abstract: We study how much a linear program (LP) or an integer program (IP) can be compressed when solved repeatedly over a fixed feasible region with varying objective coefficients. We provide a framework that compresses LP and IP formulations with guarantees on the probability of preserving optimality, using either an uncertainty set for the cost vector or historical samples. Our framework exposes a tunable tradeoff between compression and the probability of recovering an optimal solution. We characterize the minimum dimension of affine reformulations preserving the full optimizer set over a given cost region and provide sample-based learning algorithms with fast-rate guarantees, without requiring a nondegeneracy assumption for LPs. With high confidence over the training data, the learned reformulation preserves the optimizer set for an independent test cost with probability at least $1-Ï-\widetilde{O}(d^\star_Ï/n)$, where $Ï$ bounds the excluded probability mass and $d^\star_Ï$ is the retained region's decision-relevant dimension. Existing data-driven approaches to LP and IP reduction do not, to our knowledge, learn a single low-dimensional affine reformulation with a prescribed probability of preserving the full optimizer set. Experimental results show substantial improvements over the compared baselines in accuracy, sample efficiency, and computational speed.
